title: Architecture and Heritage
description: Ten texts about old buildings and the people who restore, study and argue about them: a house, a train station, a stone bridge, a new museum and more.

lessons.title: The Vampire House on Willow Street
lessons.summary: A couple spends two years restoring an old house that the neighborhood children were afraid of.
lessons.text:
When my husband and I bought the old house on Willow Street, the neighborhood children called it the vampire house. The house was built in 1889, it had a narrow tower on one corner, and for twenty years nobody had lived in it. One boy told me, quite seriously, that vampires slept in the tower and zombies walked in the garden at night. I promised him that if I met any zombies, I would ask them to leave.

What we had bought, in truth, was not a home for monsters but a tired old house. The roof leaked, so for the first winter we lived with buckets in every bedroom.

We had to decide early whether to attempt a full restoration or only a partial one. A partial restoration would have been cheaper and faster: we could have repaired the roof, painted the walls and left the rest for later. However, the longer we looked at the house, the more we wanted to give it back what it had lost. Had we known how long the work would take, we might have chosen the partial plan. I am glad we did not know.

The original decoration was the real treasure. Under layers of paint we found wooden flowers around the doors, and under an ugly carpet in the hall we found a floor of small tiles in red, cream and blue. Many of the tiles were broken, so we hired a tiler, a quiet man named Mr. Bell, who had repaired floors like ours for thirty years. The tiler spent six weeks on his knees, replacing each broken tile with a new one made in the old colors. Not once did he hurry.

I, on the other hand, was impatient. The tiler noticed this and gave me some advice: "A house this old has waited a long time. It can wait another month." I tried to be less impatient after that.

Old boards and pipes went into a large container of scrap by the garage, but the scrap wood that was still good became shelves for the kitchen.

The hardest day was the day the new bathtub arrived. The stairs are narrow, and the bathtub was not. Four people pushed, pulled and squeezed it up the stairs, an inch at a time. At one point it was squeezed so tight between the walls that we thought it would stay there forever.

Two years later, the house is finished. The roof no longer leaks, the decoration around the doors is white again, and the floor in the hall shines. Even the boy who warned me about the vampires came to see it. He looked around the hall for a long time and then told me that the vampires must have moved out.

Questions:
Why did the children call it the vampire house?
It was old, it had a narrow tower, and nobody had lived in it for twenty years.
Why were there buckets in the bedrooms?
The roof leaked, so the buckets caught the rain.
What would a partial restoration have included?
It would have included repairing the roof and painting the walls, with the rest left for later.
What did the tiler do?
He spent six weeks replacing each broken tile in the hall with a new one made in the old colors.
Why was the day the bathtub arrived so hard?
The stairs were narrow, so four people had to squeeze the bathtub up an inch at a time.

lessons.title: The Station Under the Clock
lessons.summary: A town decides to save its old train station instead of building a parking garage.
lessons.text:
For almost 50 years, Central Station in the town of Riverton was the busiest building in the region. Opened in 1912, it was a hub for 4 railway lines, and on a normal morning thousands of people dashed across its great hall to catch their trains. Passengers bought tickets at a row of wooden booths and met their friends under the station clock, which was the most beloved meeting place in town.

Then the trains slowly lost their passengers. What changed was not the station itself but the way people lived. After 1950, a great migration of families to the suburbs began, and those families drove cars. As the migration continued, fewer trains stopped in Riverton, and by 1985 only 2 trains a day still used the station. The ticket booths closed one by one. The railway company decided to abandon the building, and for years it stood empty.

In 2009, a developer offered to buy the land and build a parking garage. Many people felt that it was time to abandon the old station for good. A preliminary report by the town's engineers seemed to support the idea. According to the preliminary report, the roof was weak, the wiring was dangerous, and bringing the building into compliance with modern safety rules would cost more than building something new. Compliance with the fire code alone would require new stairs, new exits and new alarms.

Most people expected the station to be torn down. However, the tide began to turn when a retired teacher named Rosa Lind started a group called Friends of Central Station. The group asked residents to share their memories, and hundreds of stories arrived: a couple who had met under the clock, an old woman who still remembered the smell of the coffee booth. Little by little, the tide of public opinion turned. People who had not thought about the station for decades began to speak of it as a beloved part of the town's history.

The group also asked independent engineers to examine the building. Their final report disagreed with the preliminary one: the roof could be repaired, and full compliance with the fire code was possible at a reasonable cost. In 2012, exactly 100 years after the station opened, the town council voted against the parking garage.

Today the station is a hub again, though of a different kind. Trains stop there 20 times a day. The wooden booths now hold a bakery, a newspaper stand and a flower shop. Not only did the town save a building; it also gained a place where people meet once more. And every evening, under the clock, people still dash across the hall to catch their trains.

Questions:
What was Central Station like in its busiest years?
It was a hub for 4 railway lines, and thousands of people dashed across its hall every morning.
Why did the trains lose their passengers?
A great migration of families to the suburbs began, and those families drove cars.
What did the preliminary report say?
It said that compliance with modern safety rules would cost more than a new building.
How did the tide of public opinion turn?
Residents shared their memories, and people began to see the station as a beloved part of their history.
What did the final report say?
It said that the roof could be repaired and that full compliance was possible at a reasonable cost.
What is in the old wooden booths today?
They hold a bakery, a newspaper stand and a flower shop.

lessons.title: Teresa Kim: Reading Old Buildings
lessons.summary: A profile of an architect who learned from her grandmother to read buildings before changing them.
lessons.text:
The architect Teresa Kim does not like to be described as a creator of new things. "Most of my work," she says, "is helping old buildings stay alive." Over 30 years, she has restored more than 60 historic buildings, from small wooden churches to a city hall with 300 rooms.

Kim grew up in a small apartment above a shoe repair shop. Her grandmother, who lived with the family, illustrated children's books for a living, and Kim spent her childhood at her grandmother's table, watching her draw. The books her grandmother illustrated were full of castles, bridges and old towns, and every window and every stone was drawn with great care. "It was my grandmother who taught me to look," Kim says. "She used to say that a building is a story, and that you have to read it before you change it."

It is no surprise, then, that Kim was an artistic child. Her artistic talent, however, worried her parents, who wanted her to have a practical career. Architecture seemed a good compromise between the artistic and the practical, and at 18 she began a bachelor's degree in architecture.

She was soon disappointed. The curriculum, she remembers, was almost entirely about new buildings: glass towers, concrete museums, houses of steel. Old buildings appeared in the curriculum only as history, never as something an architect might actually work on. After her bachelor's degree, she spent 2 years working with stone workers, and then she returned to school for a master's degree in a specialized program on historic buildings, one of the first of its kind in the country. Today she leads a specialized team of 12 people.

Her best-known invention came from a simple problem. Old stone buildings get dirty, but the usual cleaning methods, which use strong chemicals or water at high pressure, can damage the stone. In 1998, Kim invented a soft paste of clay and water that pulls the dirt out of the stone as it dries. The invention was cheap, safe and simple, and today it is used in many countries. "I invented it so that people would use it," she says, "not so that I would get rich."

Kim has firm views on aesthetic questions. She makes a careful distinction between copying an old building and respecting it. A new part added to an old building, she believes, should not copy the old style. Its aesthetic may be fully modern, as long as its size, color and materials allow the old building to remain the most important voice.

Last year, Kim received the national Medal of Distinction for architecture. Asked what the distinction meant to her, she smiled. "My grandmother would have been prouder of my drawings than of any medal," she said. "But I think she would have liked it a little."

Questions:
What did Kim's grandmother do for a living?
She illustrated children's books.
What did her grandmother teach her?
She taught her to look, and to read a building like a story before changing it.
Why was Kim disappointed with the curriculum?
It was almost entirely about new buildings, and old buildings appeared only as history.
What did she do after her bachelor's degree?
She worked with stone workers, and then she studied in a specialized program on historic buildings.
What is her best-known invention?
It is a soft paste of clay and water that cleans old stone without damaging it.
What distinction does Kim make in aesthetic questions?
She makes a distinction between copying an old building and respecting it.

lessons.title: Review: The Harbor Museum of Art
lessons.summary: A critic reviews a new museum building that glows above the water of an old port.
lessons.text:
Few new buildings have arrived with as much hype as the Harbor Museum of Art, which opened last month at the edge of the old port. For two years, posters and online videos promised "the most beautiful building of the decade." I expected to be disappointed. I was not, although the building is not perfect.

From a distance, the museum looks like a group of white boxes placed on top of each other at different angles. At night it is lit from inside, and the boxes glow above the dark water. Seen from the old bridge, the glowing building looks like something from a fairy tale, a palace that might disappear if you looked away. Children call it "the fairy castle," and the name has already stuck.

What strikes you first is the sheer size of the place. The main hall is 40 meters high, and its back wall is made entirely of glass, so that from the entrance you look straight across the harbor to the horizon. The sheer scale of that view stops almost everyone at the door. The architect clearly wanted the sea and the sky to be part of the collection, and for once the line of the horizon feels like a work of art.

The galleries are arranged as an array of small rooms around the hall. This array gives visitors many choices; you can move from one room to the next with no single correct route. On the other hand, it is easy to get lost.

The best moment comes on the top floor. A narrow, dark passage leads into a room with mirrors on every wall, and in the middle there is a single lamp. The mirrors repeat the lamp again and again, so that it seems to stretch into an infinite line of lights. Standing in that infinite line, you feel simultaneously very small and very calm. It is a mysterious room, and its mystery is part of its charm: no sign explains it. Even after twenty minutes, it felt no less mysterious.

Not every part of the building succeeds. The restaurant is crowded and loud, and the glass elevators, which were meant to elevate visitors slowly through the hall, are so slow that many people give up and walk. The building elevates the art; it does not always elevate the comfort of the people who come to see it.

Still, the museum does something rare. It is simultaneously a home for paintings and a work of art in itself, modern and yet at home in the old port. The hype, for once, was mostly deserved. Go at night, when the boxes glow over the water, and save the mirror room for last.

Questions:
How does the museum look at night?
It is lit from inside, and its white boxes glow above the dark water.
Why do children call it "the fairy castle"?
From the old bridge, the glowing building looks like a palace from a fairy tale.
What can you see from the entrance of the main hall?
You can look straight across the harbor to the horizon through the glass wall.
What is good and bad about the array of small rooms?
It gives visitors many choices, but it is easy to get lost.
What happens in the mirror room?
The mirrors repeat a single lamp, so that it seems to stretch into an infinite line of lights.
What is the problem with the glass elevators?
They are so slow that many people give up and walk.

lessons.title: Should Towers Rise Over the Old Town?
lessons.summary: An essay weighs both sides of a plan to build two tall towers beside a historic downtown.
lessons.text:
In the old downtown of Millbrook, no building is taller than the church tower, which has stood at 50 meters since 1874. That may soon change. A developer has asked the city for permission to build two towers of 40 floors each beside the river, and the plan has divided the town. There are two serious arguments, and both deserve a fair hearing.

Those who support the towers begin with housing. Over the past 10 years, rents in Millbrook have risen by almost 60 percent, as young people have moved to the city for work. Every time a new company opens an office, rents spike again, and every spike pushes more families out. The city simply cannot accommodate all these new residents in low buildings. Two towers could accommodate 900 families on land that is now a parking lot. It is unfair, the supporters say, to tell young families that they must live an hour away so that the view of the old town stays the same.

They also point out that the church tower itself was once new. When it was built, many people thought it was too tall and too modern. The perceived clash between new and old, they argue, is often only a matter of time; what looks shocking today may look beloved in 50 years.

Those against the towers do not deny the need for accommodation. On the contrary, many of them have spent years asking the city for more affordable accommodation. Their problem is with the place, not with the homes. The old downtown is small, with narrow streets and buildings of 3 or 4 floors, and two glass towers would clash with everything around them. They also fear what is called "creep": once two towers are allowed, others will slowly creep closer to the old square, until the historic center is surrounded.

Some residents also complain about the developer's tactics. The company first presented a plan for 20 floors and only later doubled it. Critics say that such tactics are designed to make the final plan look like a compromise. Whether or not that is true, the company is now perceived as less than honest, and trust has been damaged.

What, then, is the underlying question? I believe it is not whether towers are beautiful or ugly, but who a city is for. The underlying fear on one side is that the town will lose its character; on the other side, that it will lose its young people. Both fears are reasonable. Contrary to what the loudest voices say, the choice may not be all or nothing. The towers could be built a little farther from the old square, or made lower and wider, to accommodate the same number of families without hiding the church.

Whatever the city decides, it would be unfair to call either side selfish. Both are trying to protect something they love.

Questions:
What does the developer want to build?
The developer wants to build two towers of 40 floors each beside the river.
Why do supporters say the towers are needed?
Rents have risen by almost 60 percent, and the city cannot accommodate all its new residents in low buildings.
Do the people against the towers deny the need for accommodation?
No. On the contrary, many of them have asked for more affordable accommodation for years.
Why do critics complain about the developer's tactics?
The company first presented a plan for 20 floors and later doubled it.
What does the writer think is the underlying question?
The writer thinks the underlying question is who a city is for.

lessons.title: The Bridge of 1850
lessons.summary: An engineer describes the inspection of an old stone bridge built by hand in 1850.
lessons.text:
The stone bridge over the Hollis River was built in 1850, and for more than 170 years it has carried horses, cars and school buses across the water. It has 5 arches of large gray stones, and it was built entirely by hand. Last spring, the county asked a team of engineers to find out whether the old bridge could still be trusted. I was one of them.

The place itself has a long history. Long before the town existed, buffalo crossed the river here, because the water is low and the bottom is firm. Later, the first farmers followed the same path as the buffalo, and when the town decided to build a bridge, it was natural to build it where the buffalo had crossed.

The bridge was built by a team of 8 masons led by a man named Thomas Whitfield. The masons cut every stone by hand from a hill 2 miles away and shaped it so precisely that the arches hold together mainly by their own weight. Even today, you can see each mason's personal mark, a small cross or a letter, on the stones he shaped.

Our first task was to gauge the condition of the stone. We spent 3 weeks on the bridge, wearing bright yellow helmets and safety ropes, and we examined every arch. To see inside the stones without damaging them, we used a magnetic device that finds hidden iron, and we probed the joints between the stones with thin metal rods. The magnetic device showed that the masons had placed iron pins inside some of the stones, a detail that nobody had known about. Our probes showed that most of the joints were still solid.

The bridge carries some scars. The largest scar is a long crack in the middle arch, made by the great flood of 1913, when the river was so swift that it carried whole trees against the bridge. Nevertheless, every scar we found was old and stable; none had grown in recent years.

The weather made the work harder. On foul days, when rain and wind came down the valley, the river rose quickly and became swift and dangerous. A water gauge fixed to the bridge shows the height of the river, and whenever the gauge passed 3 meters, we took off our helmets, packed our tools and waited on the shore. Over the 3 weeks, we lost 6 days to foul weather.

Our final report was simple. The bridge is safe for cars, though not for heavy trucks, and it needs a careful repair of the cracked arch. If the masons who built the bridge could see it now, I think they would be satisfied: their stones are still doing exactly what they were shaped to do.

Questions:
Why was the bridge built at this place?
The water is low and the bottom is firm, and buffalo had crossed the river here.
Who built the bridge?
A team of 8 masons led by Thomas Whitfield built it by hand.
How did the engineers look inside the stones?
They used a magnetic device that finds hidden iron, and they probed the joints with thin metal rods.
What made the largest scar on the bridge?
The great flood of 1913, when the swift river carried whole trees against the bridge.
What did the engineers do on foul days?
When the water gauge passed 3 meters, they left the bridge and waited on the shore.
What did the final report say?
It said the bridge is safe for cars but needs a repair of the cracked arch.

lessons.title: An Interview with the Town Historian
lessons.summary: A historian explains how she turned old parish records from the colonial period into a book.
lessons.text:
For the past 12 years, Ruth Hale has been the town historian of Ashford, a small town founded in 1702. This year she also finished her second term in the presidency of the Ashford Historical Society, and she has just written a book about the town's oldest building, the Ashford Parish Church, built in 1734, during the colonial period. We spoke with her in the church itself.

How did the book begin?
It began with a box. When the parish office was being repaired 5 years ago, workers found a wooden box under the floor. Inside were 3 parish record books from the colonial period, with leather bindings. The binding of the oldest book was so dry that it broke when we opened it. Rarely does a historian find colonial records in a place like that.

What is in the records?
Everything that mattered to a parish in those years: births, marriages and deaths, money spent on the roof, arguments about the seats. In colonial Ashford, families paid for their seats in church, and the best seats cost the most. People argued about those seats for years.

How do you protect such old pages?
Very carefully. Each page was photographed, and then the pages were placed in clear plastic sleeves, so that nobody's fingers touch the paper. A specialist repaired the binding. We now keep the books in a cool, dark room, and anyone who wants to read them uses the photographs.

How did you turn the records into a book?
I compiled them. For 3 years I compiled lists of every name, every date and every repair, and then I compared my lists with letters and newspapers from the same years. Compiling is slow work. What a historian needs most is not a brilliant idea but patience.

Was there a page that moved you?
Yes, a small one. In the margin of one page, a clerk had written, "The children whisper too much during the sermon." I like to imagine those children, almost 300 years ago, whispering in the same seats where children whisper today.

Have you ever made a mistake?
An embarrassing one, yes. Early in my career, I told a newspaper that the church was built in 1743. It was 1734; I had mixed up two numbers. The newspaper printed my date, and for a whole year visitors came to celebrate the wrong anniversary. It was embarrassing, but it taught me to check everything twice.

What will you do now that your presidency has ended?
I will roll up my sleeves and start the next book. The old school in Ashford is almost as old as the church, and nobody has written its history yet.

Questions:
What was found under the floor of the parish office?
Workers found a wooden box with 3 parish record books from the colonial period.
Why did families in colonial Ashford argue about seats?
They paid for their seats in church, and the best seats cost the most.
How are the old pages protected?
They were photographed and placed in clear plastic sleeves, and the books are kept in a cool, dark room.
How did Ruth Hale compile the records?
She compiled lists of every name, date and repair and compared them with letters and newspapers.
What did the clerk write in the margin?
He wrote that the children whisper too much during the sermon.
What was her embarrassing mistake?
She told a newspaper that the church was built in 1743 instead of 1734.

lessons.title: The Old Terminal Takes Off Again
lessons.summary: A grandfather takes his grandson to an old airport terminal that has become a museum of flight.
lessons.text:
The old terminal at Fairfield Airport was built in 1937, when flying was still an adventure for the rich and the brave. For 40 years, passengers walked through its round hall, showed their passports at a small desk and climbed the steps to their planes. When a larger airport opened in 1979, the terminal closed. Last year it opened again as the Fairfield Museum of Aviation, and I went there with my grandson Leo, who is 10 and wants to be a pilot.

The building itself is the first exhibit. The round hall has its original floor of black and white stone again, and the old passport desk still stands by the door. At the entrance, every child receives a paper museum passport, and Leo stamped his passport in every room he visited.

The museum tells the story of aviation in order, beginning before planes existed. The first room is filled almost entirely by a hot air balloon. Its basket hangs a few feet above the floor, and above it the huge balloon, red and gold, rises toward the ceiling. A sign explains that people were flying in balloons more than 100 years before the first plane.

The next rooms show early planes made of wood and fabric, and then the planes of the war years. One wall is covered with posters from that war. Some ask young men to become pilots; others show happy families saving money for the war. A short text explains that these posters were propaganda: they were made by the government to shape what people thought and felt. Leo asked me what propaganda meant, and I told him that it is a picture that wants you to believe something without asking questions.

Leo's favorite exhibit was a small silver plane called the Silver Streak. In 1951, a duo of pilots, two sisters named Edna and Alice Carter, flew it across the country in 31 hours. The duo took turns at the controls, and each sister slept while the other flew. A photo shows the two sisters beside the plane, laughing, with a long white streak of cloud in the sky behind them.

The last room looks beyond the sky. It shows how satellites orbit the earth, with a model satellite that slowly circles a glowing globe. A screen explains that the International Space Station orbits the earth about 16 times a day. Leo watched the model orbit the globe for ten minutes without saying a word.

For anyone who loves flying, the museum is a paradise. For Leo, it was simply paradise. Before we left, I bought him a subscription to the museum's magazine. The subscription includes 4 issues a year and free entry, so I expect we will be back soon. Had I known how much he would love the place, I would have taken him on the day it opened.

Questions:
When did the old terminal close?
It closed in 1979, when a larger airport opened.
What did Leo do with his museum passport?
He stamped his passport in every room he visited.
What does the sign in the balloon room explain?
It explains that people were flying in balloons more than 100 years before the first plane.
What does the word propaganda mean in the museum?
It means posters made by the government to shape what people thought and felt.
What did the duo of pilots do in 1951?
Two sisters, Edna and Alice Carter, flew the Silver Streak across the country in 31 hours.
What did the grandfather buy before they left?
He bought Leo a subscription to the museum's magazine.

lessons.title: From Embassy to Library
lessons.summary: A white house that was an embassy for 62 years becomes a public library.
lessons.text:
For 62 years, the large white house at the fork of Hill Road and Lake Avenue was an embassy. Built in 1905 for a rich banking family, it was sold in 1958 to a small country in the south of Europe, which used it as its embassy until 2020. The gates were locked, guards stood at the door, and surveillance cameras watched the street from every corner of the wall.

In 2020, the country moved its embassy to a modern office building near the government district. Instead of selling the old house, it made an unusual swap with the city: the country gave the city the house, and in return the city gave the country a piece of land beside the new embassy for a garden. Both sides were happy with the swap, and the city decided to turn the old embassy into a public library.

The first reaction of the people on the street was not acceptance but worry. Some were afraid of noise and traffic. At a public meeting, the mayor stood up to assure them that the library would close at 8 every evening. "I can also assure you," she said, "that your opinions will shape the design." Over the following months, acceptance grew, especially after the architects invited the residents to walk through the empty building and share their ideas.

The work took 2 years. The surveillance cameras were removed, and so were the high gates. In the old reception room, where guests once drank coffee with the ambassador, there are now long tables for reading. The large room upstairs has become a children's library, with small chairs under a painted ceiling of clouds and birds. The architects kept one surveillance camera as a piece of history. It hangs, switched off, above the main desk, with a small sign that says, "It is not watching you anymore."

The most loved feature, however, is in the garden. When the embassy staff arrived in 1958, they planted 12 olive trees from their own country. Olive trees grow slowly and can live for hundreds of years, and all 12 are still alive. Today there are benches under the olive trees, and on warm days every bench is taken.

The library opened in May. On the first morning, a line of readers stood at the gate long before it opened, and the mayor watched them walk in with obvious satisfaction. A year later, the library has more than 3,000 visits a week, and the residents who once complained have found, to their own satisfaction, that a library makes a very quiet neighbor. The road still forks in front of the white house, but these days most people who reach the fork do not walk past. They walk in.

Questions:
What was the white house like when it was an embassy?
The gates were locked, guards stood at the door, and surveillance cameras watched the street.
What swap did the country make with the city?
It gave the city the house, and the city gave it a piece of land for a garden.
What did the mayor promise the residents at the meeting?
She told them that the library would close at 8 and that their opinions would shape the design.
How did acceptance grow?
It grew after the architects invited the residents to walk through the building and share their ideas.
Why are the olive trees special?
The embassy staff planted them in 1958, and all 12 are still alive.
How do the residents feel about the library now?
They feel satisfaction, because a library makes a very quiet neighbor.

lessons.title: Saturday at the Market Hall
lessons.summary: A writer describes the traders of a restored market hall from 1886 and why she shops there.
lessons.text:
Every city has a building that its people take for granted until they almost lose it. In our city, that building is the Market Hall, a long hall of iron and glass built in 1886. For more than a century, traders sold meat, fish, cheese and vegetables under its high glass roof. By 2010, however, the roof leaked, half the tables were empty, and the city was discussing whether to sell it.

The hall was saved by a simple idea: give the traders a reason to stay. The city repaired the roof and the iron columns, cleaned the glass and cut the rent for small traders in half for 5 years. Today the hall is full again, and I go there every Saturday morning with a basket on my arm.

My first stop is always Mr. Haddad, who sells fruit, nuts and olives. He knows the supplier of every product he sells. His apples come from a farm 20 miles north, and his honey comes from a supplier who keeps bees in the hills outside the city. "If I do not know my supplier," he says, "I cannot answer my customers' questions."

Next is the cake table of Ana Ruiz. She began making cakes without sugar 10 years ago, when her father learned that he had diabetes. "People with diabetes still want cake," she says. Her cakes became so popular that she now sells them to 3 restaurants. A card beside each cake lists the calories in one slice, and I have noticed that many customers read the calories carefully, and then buy a slice anyway.

Then there is the meat counter of Sam Ortiz, whose smoked bacon is famous across the city. Every Saturday the smell of bacon fills the whole hall, because he cooks bacon sandwiches for hungry customers. I admit to a small addiction to those sandwiches. Every week I tell myself that I will stop, and every week the addiction wins. His puppy, a small brown dog named Pepper, sleeps in a basket under the counter, and children often stop to look at the puppy rather than at the meat.

Some people say that the hall is too expensive, and they have a point. A basket of food from the Market Hall costs more than the same basket from a large store. However, what I pay for is more than food. I pay for traders who know their suppliers, for bread made that morning, and for a building that has stood in the center of the city for 140 years. When the light comes through the glass roof and falls on the fruit, I think it is worth every cent.

Not until we nearly lost the hall did most of us understand how much it meant to the city.

Questions:
Why was the Market Hall in danger by 2010?
The roof leaked, half the tables were empty, and the city was discussing whether to sell it.
How did the city give the traders a reason to stay?
It repaired the hall and cut the rent for small traders in half for 5 years.
Why does Mr. Haddad want to know every supplier?
He says that if he does not know his supplier, he cannot answer his customers' questions.
Why did Ana Ruiz begin making cakes without sugar?
Her father learned that he had diabetes.
What is the writer's small addiction?
She has a small addiction to the bacon sandwiches of Sam Ortiz.
Where does the puppy sleep?
It sleeps in a basket under the counter.
